title: Column Adder
context: Grade 5, the pages on adding decimals. An adult sees steps to follow. What the pages are doing is keeping every place in its own column by lining up the points, then adding as with whole numbers, carrying across the point. Zeros after the point help keep the columns tidy; the sum is the same without them.

writeup.why: Add decimals, whole numbers among them, with the points in one line and carrying across the point, and use the order and zero properties to check a sum.
writeup.look: A column frame with one fixed point line down its middle, decimal cards lined up on it, and an answer row under a ruled line.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Column Adder' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x sixty-four, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many columns have been added, from the right. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x sixty-four, y 202. The frame spans x 110 to x 900 from y 230 to y 560, five columns 140 across headed Tens, Ones, Tenths, Hundredths and Thousandths, with the near-black point line at x 400 between Ones and Tenths. Cards sit one per row at y 270, y 350 and y 430, deep blue and labelled Given, sliding until their points sit on the line. A ruled line at y 500 has the answer row under it, where the sum is written green, labelled Sum. A column being added lights amber; a carry is a vermilion 1 labelled Carry that rolls up to the top of the next column to the left, crossing the point line when it comes from the tenths. The tray runs along y 640. The Like, Add, Point first and Swap buttons and the Add zero card stand down the right of the working area at x 960. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a point key, for setting a decimal with up to three places or typing a sum into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. A decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it. The result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum, a difference or what is left, is green, with its shaded parts. Ten of one place traded for one of the next, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written after the point to line decimals up is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded part stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the decimal point is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label, Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left or Place holder, before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last sum in the frame, every point on the one line and every carry still in vermilion above its column.

source_tool.description: A column frame fills the working area: five columns headed Tens, Ones, Tenths, Hundredths and Thousandths around one fixed near-black point line, with an answer row under a ruled line. Decimal cards, deep blue and labelled Given, drag into the frame and slide until their points sit on the point line, one card per row. A Like button can write violet zeros after the point on a shorter card, labelled Added zero, with a note that they are a help, not a rule. An Add button adds one column at a time from the right, the column lit amber; when a column makes ten or more, the ones of that total stay and a vermilion 1 labelled Carry rolls up into the next column to the left, crossing the point line when it comes from the tenths. The sum is written green in the answer row, labelled Sum, with its point dropped straight down the point line. On the third phase a whole number card has no point and will not line up until a Point first button writes a violet point after its ones digit. On the last phase a Swap button reverses the order of the cards and an Add zero card adds 0, and the sum stays as it was. A number pad sets any decimal with up to three places. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many columns have been added.
source_tool.art_direction: Two strings, measured and lined up / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: strips cut into ten equal parts, hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, place value charts with a column for each place, column sums with their points in one line, and measuring jugs, ropes and scales marked in tenths.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared or combined with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip in tenths has ten parts of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
The decimal point is drawn large and always sits between the ones and the tenths. In a column, every point lies on one vertical line.
A place value chart names every column above its digit: Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance.

Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a strip cutting into tenths, ten tenths sliding together into one whole, a zero appearing after the point, or a carry moving to the next place.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a decimal plays in a piece of working: every decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it, and every result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum or a difference, is green, with its shaded parts; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Ten of one place traded for one of the next place, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written at the end, after the point, to make like decimals is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. An unshaded part of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the decimal point itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look down the point line. Is every point on it?
voice.onNext: New numbers. Line up the points first.
voice.opening: A column frame, with one line for every point.
voice.onFinish: Every point in one line, and every carry across.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Add any decimals and whole numbers.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has measured two strings and written their lengths one below the other with the points in one line. The tool is what slides every card to the point line and rolls each carry across the point, which paper shows only finished.

answer_key.rule: Write the decimals one below the other with the points in one line, so each place is in its own column. Add as whole numbers, from the right, carrying ten of one place as one of the next, across the point too. Put the point in the sum straight below the other points. A whole number has its point after the ones digit. Zeros written after the point to make like decimals keep the columns tidy; they are a help, not a rule. Changing the order of the addends does not change the sum, and adding 0 changes nothing.
answer_key.wrong: The cards are lined up again on the point line and the columns are added one at a time from the right, each carry rolled across, with the child's sum kept in a row beside the answer row. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Write 1.6 as 1.60, so both have two decimal places. It is a help, not a rule.
Write one below the other with the points in one line.
Add as whole numbers: 3 + 0 = 3 hundredths, 2 + 6 = 8 tenths, 5 + 1 = 6 ones.
Put the point straight below the others: 5.23 + 1.60 = 6.83.
items.question: Add 5.23 and 1.6.
items.checkpoint: Line up the points, then add as whole numbers.
items.misconception: Lining up the last digits instead of the points, which adds the 6 tenths to the 3 hundredths.

steps: Hundredths: 7 + 6 = 13, so write 3 and carry 1 tenth.
Tenths: 8 + 4 + 1 = 13, so write 3 and carry 1 one across the point.
items.question: Add 2.87 and 3.46.
items.checkpoint: Ten of one place is carried as one of the next place, across the point too.
items.misconception: Forgetting the carried 1 tenth, which gives 6.23, one tenth too small.

steps: 9 is a whole number, so its point goes after the 9: 9 = 9.00.
Write 0.4 as 0.40, and line up all three points.
The point in the sum goes straight below the others.
items.question: Add 9, 1.75 and 0.4.
items.checkpoint: A whole number has its point after the ones digit.
items.misconception: Lining the 9 up under the last digit of 1.75, which adds 9 hundredths instead of 9 ones.

steps: Changing the order of the addends does not change the sum.
items.question: Does 2.06 + 5.3 give the same sum as 5.3 + 2.06?
items.checkpoint: Changing the order of the addends does not change the sum.
items.misconception: Thinking the greater number must come first, and adding again only in that order, though either order gives the same sum.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Add 1.58 and 2.34.
items.final_answer: 3.92. Hundredths: 8 + 4 = 12, so write 2 and carry 1 tenth

items.question: Add 6 and 2.35.
items.final_answer: 8.35. Write 6 as 6.00 first, with its point after the 6

items.question: Three ribbons are 4 m, 1.85 m and 0.6 m long. What is their total length?
Is 4.7 + 2.18 the same as 2.18 + 4.7? What is the sum?

teaching_notes: The points go in one line, one below the other; that is what keeps each place in its own column. Writing zeros after the point to make like decimals keeps the columns tidy, and the sum is the same without them. A carry from the tenths goes into the ones, straight across the point. A whole number has its point after the ones digit; write it there before lining up. Check a sum by adding in another order.
generation_prompt: Build a decimal addition tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A column frame fills the working area, columns headed Tens, Ones, Tenths, Hundredths and Thousandths around one fixed near-black point line, with an answer row under a ruled line. Deep blue decimal cards labelled Given drag into the frame and slide until their points sit on the point line. A Like button writes violet zeros after the point, labelled Added zero, as a help. An Add button adds one column at a time from the right, lit amber; a total of ten or more leaves its ones and rolls a vermilion 1 labelled Carry into the next column, across the point line from the tenths. The sum is written green, labelled Sum. A whole number card will not line up until a Point first button writes a violet point after its ones digit. A Swap button and an Add zero card leave the sum as it was. A number pad. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of columns added. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right.
